summary: Defines a common format for exchanging secondary school transcripts by email. It uses existing standards to prevent alteration of the content and to deliver transcripts securely from students to their chosen recipients without third parties.

eli5.summary: A student can email their school report straight to a college in a form that cannot be secretly changed.

questions: how to email school transcripts securely
what is the transcript email format
how to send school transcripts by email securely
subtitle: A secure way for students to email their school transcripts to colleges and employers

tldr.problem: School transcript distribution increasingly relies on third-party processors that intercept and monitor student communications. Students have lost control of their own records and privacy.
tldr.mechanism: EESST (Email Exchange of Secondary School Transcripts) allows schools to digitally sign transcripts and students to encrypt and email them directly to recipients using standard OpenPGP cryptography. Recipients verify the signature and decrypt the content independently.
tldr.outcome: Students regain control and privacy: they distribute their own transcripts, third parties cannot monitor their applications, and recipients can verify authenticity without mediators.

today: RFC 7681 defines the EESST protocol as an informational standard. While adoption has been limited, the RFC provides a complete, implementable specification for privacy-preserving transcript exchange that students and schools could adopt to eliminate third-party intermediaries.

sections.title: From Paper Seals to Third-Party Processors
sections.content:
Traditionally, paper transcripts protected student privacy: a guidance counselor signed and sealed an envelope, the student sent it where they wanted, and nobody else saw it. But schools introduced third-party processors to automate distribution. Now schools send transcripts to a central server, the server handles distribution, and the processor monitors and controls where transcripts go.

This breaks student privacy, violates the end-to-end principle, and creates a data-harvesting opportunity for the processor. Students are coerced into a choice: surrender privacy or use a slow manual system. The processor gains unfettered control over personal records that should remain private.

RFC 7681 automates the traditional process electronically: the school digitally signs each transcript and gives it to the student. The student encrypts and emails it to chosen recipients using existing, standards-based secure email. No third party is needed.
sections.eli5: Schools used to seal transcripts in envelopes and hand them to students. Then companies convinced schools to let them control the distribution instead. This RFC brings back the student's control by using digital signatures and encryption.

sections.title: Design Principles: Student Control and End-to-End
sections.content:
The protocol prioritizes student needs first. Students need credible documents (cryptographically signed by the school so recipients know they are authentic) and privacy (encrypted so only intended recipients see the content). After students, the protocol addresses recipient needs: they must independently verify signature and integrity and may need to extract and process transcript data. Finally, it addresses school needs: reducing cost of preparation and meeting legal obligations to protect student privacy.

The design strictly follows the end-to-end principle. Communication flows directly from school to student to recipient. No central authority mediates. The school does not know who receives transcripts; neither the school nor any third party is responsible for tracking distribution. The student bears primary responsibility for privacy in transit, incentivizing careful choices about recipient public keys and potentially requesting key certifications.

Formal request protocols are not needed: when a student directly controls distribution, they have the strongest incentive in successful delivery and will act if communication fails. SMTP's fail-safe delivery model provides automatic feedback.
sections.eli5: The design trusts students to send their own transcripts and trusts email to deliver them. No third party monitors or controls the process.

sections.title: Roles: Originator, Student, and Recipient
sections.content:
Three roles participate. The transcript originator (usually a guidance counselor or school administrator) creates and digitally signs transcripts using an OpenPGP key pair. The originator must securely store the private key, publish the public key with its fingerprint, and create a key revocation certificate. Originators are responsible only for creating transcripts and presenting them confidentially to individual students—not for distributing them.

The student receives the signed transcript and distributes it. The student must create a personal email account, discover each recipient's email address and OpenPGP public key, import those keys into an OpenPGP database, and use an email client supporting OpenPGP/MIME to encrypt and transmit the transcript. The student is solely responsible for choosing recipients and ensuring privacy in transit.

The transcript recipient (a college admissions office or employer) generates an OpenPGP key pair for receiving transcripts, publishes their public key and a dedicated email address, maintains a collection of legitimate originator public keys, and receives, decrypts, and validates received transcripts using OpenPGP/MIME-capable email software. Recipients must reject transcripts showing signs of non-student transmission (multiple transcripts in one message, originator as sender, originator also signing the transmission, or multiple recipients).
sections.eli5: School makes and signs the transcript. Student encrypts and sends it. Recipient decrypts and checks the signature. Each party has their own OpenPGP key.

sections.title: Transcript Content and Signed Format
sections.content:
Transcript content is a multipart/mixed MIME structure with exactly three parts: a preface (plain text with commentary about validation and interpretation), a computational transcript (XML in PESC format for automated processing), and a display transcript (PDF for human review). Each part is identified by required MIME headers: Content-Type, Content-Description, MIME-Version, Eesst-Version, From (identifying originator and key), Organization (the school), Subject (optional), and Date.

The computational transcript uses PESC (Postsecondary Electronic Standards Council) XML schemas. Critically, a transcript originator MUST NOT brand specific destination recipients onto transcripts. The Destination element must contain only an empty Organization tag, assuring students can distribute copies without the originator monitoring their choices. Originators MAY omit sensitive information (social security numbers, family details, race, ethnicity) to protect privacy.

A signed school transcript wraps the content in a multipart/signed MIME structure per OpenPGP/MIME. It comprises exactly two parts: the transcript content and an application/pgp-signature part containing the originator's digital signature. The Eesst-Version header serves dual purposes: it identifies the EESST format version and allows simple, unambiguous detection of signed school transcripts while enabling verification using familiar email clients.
sections.eli5: A transcript is a MIME package with three files inside: a cover letter, XML data for computers, and a PDF for humans. Then the school signs the whole package with their digital signature.

sections.title: Transmission Formats: Encrypted, Signed, File, and Inline
sections.content:
The RFC defines four transmission formats. Encrypted Format sends the signed transcript as an attachment to an OpenPGP encrypted email (multipart/encrypted with application/pgp-encrypted and application/octet-stream parts). Encrypted and Signed Format adds a second layer: the student signs the transmission with their own key, then encrypts it, creating nested signatures (originator's signature inside, student's outside).

When the transmitting computer cannot be trusted (like school-provided computers or web-based email), Encrypted File Format lets the student encrypt the transcript on a trusted computer, transfer the encrypted binary file to an untrusted computer via USB, then attach it to a plaintext email as application/octet-stream. The recipient detaches and decrypts the file locally. Traditional Inline Format similarly allows encryption on a trusted computer, but transfers the ASCII-armored encrypted text for pasting into an untrusted email client's message body.

Recipients MUST accept all four formats and MUST detect and reject transmission characteristics indicating non-student transmission: multiple transcripts in one message, originator as sender, originator also signing the transmission, or multiple recipients.
sections.eli5: Students can send transcripts four ways: fully encrypted email, encrypted plus signed email, encrypted file attached, or encrypted text pasted inline. All work, but the last two suit untrusted computers.

sections.title: Keeping Keys and Transcripts Safe
sections.content:
The protocol's security depends entirely on OpenPGP implementation and key management. Originators and recipients must use SHA-256 for digests and RSA keys of at least 2048 bits. The originator's private key must remain secret; the guidance director should be physically present during transcript signing. Both originators and recipients must create and securely store key revocation certificates.

Public keys must be published with fingerprints on institutional web pages or in the global OpenPGP key database. Recipients should resist forgery by asking trustworthy individuals (colleagues or officials) to sign their public key, creating a web of trust. Students bear ultimate responsibility for evaluating key authenticity before encrypting their transcript.

Cryptographic operations must occur in private on isolated, controlled computers to protect confidentiality. Using thin clients or web-based computing forfeits the protocol's protections. Recipients should not auto-reply to transcript transmissions, as such replies could provide valuable feedback to attackers.
sections.eli5: Keep private keys secret and on trusted computers. Share public keys widely with fingerprints so people know they are real. Don't auto-reply to transcripts.
